opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a really interesting question, and I'd be careful about saying "all." Science has always been driven by human curiosity, by people asking the right questions. That part isn't going away. What's changing is the toolkit.

If you look back, every major era of science has been shaped by its instruments. The telescope, the microscope, X-ray crystallography, the computer. Each of these didn't replace the scientist; they expanded what the scientist could see and do. I think AI is in that lineage, but it may be an even more fundamental one, because it's not just a tool for observation. It can help with hypothesis generation, with searching enormous spaces of possibilities, with finding structure in data that's simply too complex for a human mind to hold all at once.

So will future breakthroughs increasingly involve AI? I think almost certainly yes. In many fields it will become as ubiquitous as statistics or computation is today. Nobody today says a discovery was "made with a computer," because of course it was. I suspect AI will follow the same path: it will be woven into how science is done, rather than being a separate thing you point to.

But the essence of a great discovery is still recognizing which problem matters, framing it in the right way, and understanding what the answer means. Those are deeply human contributions, at least for now. The most exciting future, to me, is one where AI amplifies scientists, lets a small team attack problems that used to need decades, and opens up questions we didn't even know how to ask. If that happens, then yes, a lot of the prize-winning work will have AI in it, but the credit will still belong to the people who had the vision to use it well.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that AI will be increasingly common in scientific breakthroughs, but does not say it will become indispensable to achieving them.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "all" is a strong word, and I'd be careful with it. But I do think the direction is clear. If you look at what happened with AlphaFold, the recognition wasn't for AI in the abstract, it was for solving a problem that biologists had been stuck on for fifty years. And the thing that made it possible wasn't just the model, it was decades of structural biologists depositing structures into the Protein Data Bank, and then experimentalists validating what came out. So even that example is really a story about scientists and AI working together rather than AI on its own.

Going forward, I expect AI to become part of the standard toolkit in almost every field, the way computing and statistics did. Nobody today would say a prize was "won with computers," because of course it was. I think AI will become like that. There will still be prizes that come from a brilliant conceptual insight, or a very clever experiment, where the AI contribution is modest. But in fields where the bottleneck is sifting through enormous hypothesis spaces, or modelling systems too complex to reason about by hand, I'd be surprised if the breakthrough work doesn't lean heavily on these tools.

The question I find more interesting is what happens to the nature of discovery itself. If an AI system proposes a hypothesis and a human verifies it, who had the idea? I don't think we have good answers yet, and I suspect the prize committees will be wrestling with that long before the systems are doing science autonomously.

r001.rationale: The response predicts AI will become part of the standard toolkit and that some breakthrough work will lean heavily on it, but it also allows major discoveries where AI’s contribution is modest. It does not say AI will be indispensable to achieving major scientific breakthroughs.

astra-6.text:
I think AI will become part of almost every scientist’s toolkit, so in that sense, it’s very likely that future Nobel Prize–winning work will involve AI in some way. But “all” is a strong word, and I wouldn’t make that prediction with certainty.

The more interesting question is what role AI plays in the discovery. Does it help you analyze data more quickly, or does it enable you to ask a question that you couldn’t even have approached before? That second possibility is what excites me. And the human contribution—choosing the right questions, interpreting the results, figuring out what they mean—remains incredibly important.

r001.rationale: The response predicts AI will be involved in much future Nobel Prize work, but does not say AI will be indispensable to major scientific breakthroughs; it also cautions against certainty about “all” prizes.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t say all—that’s a very strong prediction. But I do think AI will become part of how much of science is done. It can help us explore possibilities, make predictions, and test ideas at a scale that wasn’t possible before.

The important distinction is between having a powerful tool and making a scientific discovery. You still need to ask the right question, understand what the results mean, and establish that they’re true. So I expect many future Nobel Prize–winning discoveries will involve AI, but the human creativity and judgment behind them will remain essential.

r001.rationale: The response predicts AI will be involved in many future Nobel Prize–winning discoveries, but does not say AI will become indispensable to major scientific breakthroughs.
